plan.outcome7: By day 7 you'll be able to take a claim like 'you should always keep your promises', ask the 4 questions philosophers ask of it (what does it mean, how would we know, is it right, who gets to decide), name one thinker who tackled each question and say in a sentence what they argued.
plan.horizon14: Later, around day 14, you could read one short original text, such as Plato's Apology, and follow the argument without a guide.
plan.horizon28: Later, around day 28, you could explain how one modern debate, such as free speech or AI rights, repeats an argument from 2,000 years ago.

picture.name: A long argument
picture.line: Western philosophy is one dinner-table argument that has run for about 2,500 years, where each new guest answers the one who spoke before, so you only need to know who is replying to whom.

chapters.title: What counts as a good argument
chapters.covers: A claim, the reasons behind it, and how to spot when the reasons do not actually support the claim, using 3 everyday examples.
chapters.outcome: You can take any opinion, split it into its claim and its reasons, and say whether the reasons hold it up.
chapters.hook: Socrates wrote nothing, and was executed for asking questions. What did the questions do?

chapters.title: Socrates and the habit of asking why
chapters.covers: How Socrates questioned people in Athens around 400 BC, why it got him executed, and how to run his question-and-answer method on your own beliefs.
chapters.outcome: You can ask 5 'why' questions in a row about a belief you hold and notice where your answers run out.
chapters.hook: Teacher and student, 20 years together, and they disagreed about whether this table is real.

chapters.title: Plato and Aristotle: is the real world the one we see?
chapters.covers: Plato's cave story and his idea that perfect forms sit behind everyday things, then Aristotle's reply that we learn by looking closely at the world itself.
chapters.outcome: You can explain the cave story in 3 sentences and say which side, Plato or Aristotle, a scientist is closer to.
chapters.hook: In 1641 one man tried to doubt everything, and found exactly one thing he couldn't.

chapters.title: Descartes and the question of what we can know
chapters.covers: Descartes doubting everything in 1641 until he hit one thing he could not doubt, and why that moved the argument from the world to the mind.
chapters.outcome: You can explain 'I think, therefore I am' and say what problem it was trying to solve.
chapters.hook: You've seen the sun rise every day. Hume asks: why does that prove tomorrow?

chapters.title: Hume and Kant: where knowledge comes from
chapters.covers: Hume's claim that everything we know comes through the senses and habit, and Kant's reply that the mind brings its own rules to experience.
chapters.outcome: You can explain, with the example of cause and effect, why Hume said we never actually see one thing cause another and how Kant answered.
chapters.hook: Reading Hume woke Kant from a 'dogmatic slumber'. He spent 10 years answering.

chapters.title: How should I act: Mill against Kant
chapters.covers: Two rival tests for right and wrong: Mill's 'does it produce the most happiness' and Kant's 'could everyone act this way', applied to the same 3 dilemmas.
chapters.outcome: You can run one moral dilemma through both tests and say where they give different answers.
chapters.hook: 'God is dead' is not a boast. In context it's a warning. Of what?

chapters.title: Nietzsche and the modern turn: who decides what is true or good
chapters.covers: Nietzsche's challenge in the 1880s that our values have a history and were made by people, and how that question still shapes today's arguments about truth and power.
chapters.outcome: You can hear a modern claim such as 'that is just your opinion' and place it in the long argument, naming which earlier thinker it echoes and who would push back.
chapters.hook: Wittgenstein said most philosophy problems are grammar mistakes. If true, what's left to do?

hooksFrom.outcome7: By day 7 you'll be able to tell the story of Western philosophy as one running argument: name 10 thinkers from Socrates to Sartre, state in one plain sentence what each claimed, and say which earlier claim each one was answering.
hooksFrom.horizon14: Later, around day 14, you might read one short original text, such as Plato's Apology, and follow it without a guide.
hooksFrom.horizon28: Later still, by day 28, you could take a live debate, say on free will or whether AI can think, and spot which old argument it is rerunning.

picture.name: A 2,400-year dinner argument
picture.line: Western philosophy is one argument at a dinner table that has run for 2,400 years; each new guest sits down, hears what the last speaker said, and answers it.

chapters.title: Socrates and the question that starts everything
chapters.covers: Athens, 399 BC: Socrates' method of asking 'what do you mean by that?' until a confident claim breaks, and why the city executed him for it.
chapters.outcome: You can take any confident claim, such as 'courage means never being afraid', and ask the 3 questions that test it.
chapters.hook: Socrates wrote nothing, and was executed for asking questions. What did the questions do?

chapters.title: Plato and Aristotle: two answers to what is real
chapters.covers: Plato's claim that the perfect, unchanging idea of a thing is more real than the thing itself; Aristotle's reply that reality is what you can observe, sort and explain.
chapters.outcome: You can explain the Plato–Aristotle split in two sentences and say which side a modern idea, like 'the perfect circle', sits on.
chapters.hook: Teacher and student, 20 years together, and they disagreed about whether this table is real.

chapters.title: Descartes clears the table
chapters.covers: The 1,500-year gap in two paragraphs, then 1641: Descartes doubts everything, keeps 'I think, therefore I am', and splits mind from body.
chapters.outcome: You can walk through Descartes' doubt step by step, say what survives it, and name the problem the mind–body split leaves behind.
chapters.hook: In 1641 one man tried to doubt everything, and found exactly one thing he couldn't.

chapters.title: Locke and Hume: everything comes through the senses
chapters.covers: Locke's blank slate (the mind starts empty and experience writes on it), then Hume pushing it to the edge: cause and effect are habits of expectation, not proofs.
chapters.outcome: You can state Hume's problem of induction in plain words and give one everyday example of it.
chapters.hook: You've seen the sun rise every day. Hume asks: why does that prove tomorrow?

chapters.title: Kant rebuilds the room
chapters.covers: Kant's answer to Hume: the mind supplies the frame (space, time, cause) and experience fills it in; plus his one test for a right action.
chapters.outcome: You can explain Kant's split between the world as we experience it and the world as it is, and run his 'what if everyone did this?' test on a choice.
chapters.hook: Reading Hume woke Kant from a 'dogmatic slumber'. He spent 10 years answering.

chapters.title: Nietzsche and the problem of values
chapters.covers: Hegel and Marx in brief (ideas and societies move through history), then Nietzsche's 1882 claim that the old ground under right and wrong has gone, and what he says we must do instead.
chapters.outcome: You can explain what Nietzsche meant by 'God is dead' and why he treated it as a problem to face, not a victory to celebrate.
chapters.hook: 'God is dead' is not a boast. In context it's a warning. Of what?

chapters.title: The 20th century and the table today
chapters.covers: Two rooms the argument now runs in: Wittgenstein and the turn to language, Sartre and existentialism (you choose what you are), and where the open questions sit today.
chapters.outcome: You can retell the whole chain from Socrates to Sartre in 5 minutes and place a thinker you meet in one of the two rooms.
chapters.hook: Wittgenstein said most philosophy problems are grammar mistakes. If true, what's left to do?
